items.title: The Satavahanas (Andhras) — Deccan's First Great Kingdom
items.body:
## The Satavahanas (Andhras)

**In one line:** The Satavahanas were the first large kingdom to rule the Deccan after the Mauryan Empire collapsed, and because the Puranas call them the **Andhras**, they are treated as the starting point of Andhra Pradesh's imperial history.

**The story**
When the Mauryan Empire broke up (after about 185 BCE), no single power controlled the **Deccan** — the dry plateau of peninsular India between the Narmada and Krishna rivers. Around the **2nd century BCE** a local Deccan family, the Satavahanas, filled that gap and built the region's first big state. They governed from **two capitals**: **Pratishthana (modern Paithan, in Maharashtra)** in the west and **Amaravati (in the Krishna valley of Andhra Pradesh)** in the east. Because they sat between the Sanskritic north and the Tamil south, they acted as a **cultural and political bridge**, carrying northern traditions south and absorbing local Deccan ways.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC treats the Satavahanas as the foundation of Andhra's recorded history — the Puranas literally name them the Andhras — so identity, capitals and extent are repeat prelims facts.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Puranic name | Andhras |
| Period | c. 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE |
| Capitals | Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati |
| Realm | Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh |
| Role | Bridge between North and South India |

**Terms explained**
- **Deccan** — the plateau of southern India; the Satavahana heartland.
- **Puranas** — ancient Sanskrit texts of myth, genealogy and history; they list the Satavahanas as the Andhra dynasty.
- **Pratishthana** — the old name of Paithan on the Godavari, the western capital.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Andhras** here = the Satavahana dynasty of the Puranas, NOT the modern state of Andhra Pradesh (named much later).
- **Pratishthana (Paithan)** is in Maharashtra; **Amaravati** is in Andhra Pradesh — two different capitals, not one place.

**Remember it:** Two capitals, one dynasty — 'Paithan in the west, Amaravati in the east'.

**TL;DR**
- Satavahanas = the Andhras of the Puranas; first major Deccan power (c. 2nd century BCE).
- Twin capitals: Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati.
- Ruled modern AP, Telangana, Maharashtra, Karnataka and MP.
- Acted as a bridge between North and South India.

figure.alt: Map of the Satavahana Empire in the Deccan with Pratishthana and Amaravati marked
figure.caption: The Satavahana Empire spanned the Deccan with centres at Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati, bridging north and south India.

keyPoints: Most significant Deccan power after the Mauryas (c. 2nd century BCE).
Called Andhras in the Puranas; built the first major Deccan kingdom.
Ruled modern AP, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and MP.
Twin capitals: Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati.
Acted as a political and cultural bridge between North and South India.
items.mnemonic: Andhras of the Deccan — two capitals: 'Paithan in the west, Amaravati in the east'.

items.title: Simuka — Founder of the Dynasty
items.body:
## Simuka — the Founder (c. 60 BCE – 37 BCE)

**In one line:** Simuka is the king who started the Satavahana dynasty, and we know him mainly from the Naneghat inscription.

**The story**
After the Mauryas, the Deccan was held by scattered local chiefs and by the northern **Shungas**. **Simuka** defeated rivals in Maharashtra and Andhra and welded a kingdom together. He did not do it alone — he leaned on **alliances with the Rathikas and Bhojakas**, two local warrior clans, to build early strength. His rise **ended Shunga control in the Deccan**. When he died he was followed not by a son but by his **brother Kanha (also written Krishna)**, who extended the new state.

**Why it is asked**
'Founder of the Satavahanas' is a direct one-mark fact, and the succession twist (brother, not son) is a classic trap in statement-based questions.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Role | Founder of the dynasty |
| Allies | Rathikas and Bhojakas |
| Achievement | Ended Shunga control in the Deccan |
| Named in | Naneghat inscription |
| Successor | His brother Kanha (Krishna) |

**Terms explained**
- **Shungas** — the Brahmin dynasty that ruled from Magadha after the Mauryas; Simuka pushed them out of the Deccan.
- **Naneghat inscription** — a Satavahana record in a hill pass near Pune that lists early kings.
- **Rathikas and Bhojakas** — local Deccan clans whose support helped Simuka.

**Don't confuse**
- Simuka was succeeded by his **brother Kanha**, NOT by his son Satakarni I.
- Simuka (founder) is different from **Satakarni I** (a later conqueror) and **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (the greatest king).

**Remember it:** 'Simuka Started it — with the Rathikas and Bhojakas, named at Naneghat, handed to his brother'.

**TL;DR**
- Simuka founded the Satavahana dynasty (c. 60–37 BCE).
- Allied with the Rathikas and Bhojakas; ended Shunga control in the Deccan.
- Named in the Naneghat inscription.
- Succeeded by his brother Kanha (Krishna), not a son.
keyPoints: Simuka is the founder of the Satavahana dynasty.
Defeated local rulers in Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh.
Allied with the Rathikas and Bhojakas.
Mentioned in the Naneghat inscription; ended Shunga control in the Deccan.
Succeeded by his brother Kanha (Krishna).
items.mnemonic: Founder Simuka — 'Started with the Rathikas & Bhojakas, named in Naneghat'.

items.title: Satakarni I — Lord of Dakshinapatha
items.body:
## Satakarni I — Lord of Dakshinapatha

**In one line:** Satakarni I was the first great conqueror of the dynasty, who pushed north into Malwa and took the proud title 'Lord of Dakshinapatha' (lord of the southern route).

**The story**
Coming after the founder Simuka and his brother Kanha, **Satakarni I** turned the young kingdom into an expanding power. He defeated local rulers and extended control into the **Malwa and Narmada** regions to the north. To announce that he was now a sovereign ruler, he performed **two Ashvamedha (horse) sacrifices** — the old Vedic ritual by which a king claimed overlordship. His queen **Nayanika (Naganika)** recorded his power in the **Naneghat inscription**, which gives him the title **Lord of Dakshinapatha**. His reach also brought him into **conflict with Kharavela of Kalinga**, whose **Hathigumpha inscription** mentions a Satakarni.

**Why it is asked**
The title 'Lord of Dakshinapatha', the two Ashvamedhas and the Naneghat–Nayanika link are all stock prelims hooks, often mixed up with later kings.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Place in line | Third ruler, after Kanha |
| Expansion | Malwa and the Narmada valley |
| Title | Lord of Dakshinapatha |
| Rituals | Two Ashvamedha sacrifices |
| Recorded by | Queen Nayanika (Naneghat inscription) |
| Rival | Kharavela of Kalinga (Hathigumpha) |

**Terms explained**
- **Dakshinapatha** — the great southern trade route and, by extension, the whole Deccan; 'Lord of Dakshinapatha' means master of the south.
- **Ashvamedha** — the Vedic horse sacrifice a king performed to assert sovereignty.
- **Hathigumpha inscription** — the record of King Kharavela of Kalinga, which names a Satakarni.

**Don't confuse**
- **Satakarni I** (early conqueror, 'Lord of Dakshinapatha') is NOT **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (the much later greatest ruler).
- The **Naneghat** inscription (Nayanika, for Satakarni I) is different from the **Nasik Prashasti** (Gautami Balashri, for Gautamiputra).

**Remember it:** 'Satakarni I = South's lord who ran TWO horse sacrifices' — remembered by Queen Nayanika at Naneghat.

**TL;DR**
- Satakarni I expanded into Malwa and the Narmada valley.
- Took the title 'Lord of Dakshinapatha'; performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices.
- His queen Nayanika recorded him in the Naneghat inscription.
- Clashed with Kharavela of Kalinga (Hathigumpha inscription).
keyPoints: Expanded into Malwa and the Narmada valley.
Titled 'Lord of Dakshinapatha' (southern route).
Naneghat inscription written by his queen Nayanika (Naganika).
Performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices to assert sovereignty.
Mentioned in the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela of Kalinga.
items.mnemonic: Satakarni I = 'Dakshinapatha lord who ran two Ashvamedhas' — remembered by Queen Nayanika at Naneghat.

items.title: Hala — Patron of Literature
items.body:
## Hala — the Poet-King (c. 20 CE – 24 CE)

**In one line:** Hala was a Satavahana king remembered not for conquests but for compiling the Gatha Saptasati, a famous anthology of Prakrit love poems.

**The story**
Not every Satavahana king was a warrior. **Hala** ruled a short, **peaceful reign** and spent it on culture rather than war. He compiled (and partly composed) the **Gatha Saptasati** — literally 'Seven Hundred Verses' — a collection of short **love poems in Maharashtri Prakrit**, the everyday language of the western Deccan. The work paints village life, love and the seasons, and it tells us the Satavahana court used Prakrit, not Sanskrit, as its literary language. The **Matsya Purana** remembers Hala as a notable king, which is how later tradition kept his name alive.

**Why it is asked**
'Which king wrote the Gatha Saptasati?' and 'In which language?' are repeat facts; the pairing of Hala with Prakrit is the point.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Known for | Compiling the Gatha Saptasati |
| Theme | Love poems / village life |
| Language | Maharashtri Prakrit |
| Reign | Short and peaceful |
| Remembered in | Matsya Purana |

**Terms explained**
- **Gatha Saptasati** (also Gaha Sattasai) — 'Seven Hundred Verses', an anthology of short love poems.
- **Maharashtri Prakrit** — a popular spoken language of the Deccan, used in place of Sanskrit at the Satavahana court.
- **Matsya Purana** — one of the eighteen great Puranas; it lists Satavahana kings including Hala.

**Don't confuse**
- Hala wrote the **Gatha Saptasati** (Prakrit poetry); he did NOT write the Nasik Prashasti (that is Gautami Balashri's inscription).
- Hala is a **literary** king, not a conqueror like Satakarni I or Gautamiputra.

**Remember it:** 'Hala the poet — 700 Prakrit love verses (Gatha Saptasati)'.

**TL;DR**
- Hala compiled the Gatha Saptasati, 700 love poems in Maharashtri Prakrit.
- His reign was peaceful, focused on literature.
- He is remembered in the Matsya Purana.
- Shows the Satavahana court used Prakrit as its literary language.
keyPoints: Compiled the Gatha Saptasati, a Maharashtri Prakrit anthology of love poems.
Remembered as a patron of literature; mentioned in the Matsya Purana.
His reign was peaceful, centred on culture rather than conquest.
items.mnemonic: Hala the poet-king — 'Gatha Saptasati = 700 love verses in Prakrit'.

items.title: Gautamiputra Satakarni — The Greatest Satavahana
items.body:
## Gautamiputra Satakarni (c. 106 CE – 130 CE)

**In one line:** Gautamiputra Satakarni is counted the greatest Satavahana ruler because he rescued the dynasty from the Shakas and rebuilt its power.

**The story**
Before him, foreign-origin rulers — the **Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas** — had eaten into Satavahana lands from the north-west. **Gautamiputra Satakarni** reversed this: he **defeated the Shaka king Nahapana** (and even restruck Nahapana's silver coins) and drove back the Pahlavas and Yavanas, stretching his empire from **Malwa, Saurashtra and Konkan to Vidarbha and the Krishna River**. His story survives because his mother, **Gautami Balashri**, had it carved as the **Nasik Prashasti** (a prashasti is a praise-inscription). It calls him **Ekabrahmana — 'the unique Brahmin'** — and the king who restored the pride of the Brahmins and the varna order. Yet he was not narrow: the same reign **granted land to Buddhist monks**, a sign of religious balance.

**Why it is asked**
Gautamiputra + Nahapana, Ekabrahmana, and the Nasik Prashasti by Gautami Balashri are among the most-asked Satavahana facts in APPSC and other exams.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Reputation | Greatest Satavahana ruler |
| Key victory | Defeated the Shaka king Nahapana |
| Also beat | Pahlavas and Yavanas |
| Empire | Malwa, Saurashtra, Konkan to Vidarbha and the Krishna |
| Source | Nasik Prashasti, by his mother Gautami Balashri |
| Title | Ekabrahmana ('the unique Brahmin') |
| Religion | Championed Brahmanism, yet gave land to Buddhist monks |

**Terms explained**
- **Shakas, Pahlavas, Yavanas** — foreign-origin ruling groups (Scythians, Parthians and Greeks) in north-west India.
- **Nahapana** — the Western Shaka (Kshaharata) king whom Gautamiputra defeated.
- **Nasik Prashasti** — a praise-inscription at Nasik recording his deeds; written by his mother Gautami Balashri.
- **Ekabrahmana** — 'the unique/peerless Brahmin', his title in that inscription.

**Don't confuse**
- **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (greatest, c. 106–130 CE) is NOT **Satakarni I** (early 'Lord of Dakshinapatha').
- He defeated **Nahapana**; the Rudradaman I marriage alliance belongs to his successor Vashishtiputra Pulumavi.

**Remember it:** 'Gautamiputra = Greatest — beat the three foreigners (Shakas, Pahlavas, Yavanas); mother Gautami Balashri wrote the Nasik Prashasti'.

**TL;DR**
- Greatest Satavahana ruler; revived the empire (c. 106–130 CE).
- Defeated the Shaka king Nahapana, plus Pahlavas and Yavanas.
- Nasik Prashasti by his mother Gautami Balashri; titled Ekabrahmana.
- Championed Brahmanism yet gave land grants to Buddhist monks.

figure.alt: Illustrative banner depicting a Satavahana warrior king with the title Satavahana Dynasty
figure.caption: Gautamiputra Satakarni revived Satavahana power, defeating the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas — celebrated in the Nasik Prashasti of Gautami Balashri.

keyPoints: Greatest/most powerful Satavahana ruler; revived the empire.
Defeated the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas — including the Shaka king Nahapana.
Nasik Prashasti inscribed by his mother Gautami Balashri.
Called Ekabrahmana ('the unique Brahmin'); restored Brahmin pride.
Empire from Malwa/Saurashtra/Konkan to Vidarbha and the Krishna River.
Still made land grants to Buddhist monks — religious harmony.
items.mnemonic: Gautamiputra = 'Greatest' — beat the 3 foreigners (Shakas, Pahlavas, Yavanas); his mother Gautami Balashri wrote the Nasik Prashasti.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Gautamiputra Satakarni – The Reviver of Satavahana Power)

items.title: Vashishtiputra Pulumavi & Yajna Sri Satakarni
items.body:
## The Later Great Rulers

**In one line:** Pulumavi pushed Satavahana power to the Krishna delta and made peace with the Shakas by marriage, while Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last strong king who won back lost land.

**The story**
After Gautamiputra came his son **Vashishtiputra Pulumavi (c. 130 CE – 154 CE)**. He extended the empire's southern edge to the **mouth of the Krishna River** and issued **coins showing ships**, a hint that he encouraged **overseas trade**. To settle the long Shaka rivalry he **married the daughter of the Shaka ruler Rudradaman I** — a marriage recorded in Rudradaman's **Junagadh inscription**, an early example of marital diplomacy. Decades later, **Yajna Sri Satakarni (c. 165 CE – 194 CE)** was the **last great Satavahana**; he **recovered Malwa and Konkan from the Shakas** and, like Pulumavi, left **ship-motif coins** pointing to busy sea trade. After him the empire weakened and split apart.

**Why it is asked**
The Pulumavi–Rudradaman marriage (Junagadh), ship coins, and 'last great ruler = Yajna Sri' are recurring prelims pairings.

**Picture it**

| Ruler | Period | Remembered for |
|---|---|---|
| Vashishtiputra Pulumavi | c. 130–154 CE | Krishna delta; ship coins; married Rudradaman I's daughter (Junagadh) |
| Yajna Sri Satakarni | c. 165–194 CE | Last great ruler; recovered Malwa and Konkan; ship coins |

**Terms explained**
- **Junagadh inscription** — the rock inscription of the Shaka king Rudradaman I; it mentions the marriage link with the Satavahanas.
- **Rudradaman I** — the powerful Western Shaka (Kshatrapa) ruler of Saurashtra.
- **Ship-motif coins** — coins stamped with a two-masted ship, evidence of maritime trade.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Rudradaman marriage** is Pulumavi's, NOT Gautamiputra's (Gautamiputra fought the Shakas).
- **Yajna Sri** is the LAST great ruler; **Gautamiputra** is the greatest — different kings.

**Remember it:** 'Pulumavi = ships + Rudradaman's daughter (Junagadh); Yajna Sri = last great, ships again'.

**TL;DR**
- Pulumavi (c. 130–154 CE) reached the Krishna delta; ship coins; married Rudradaman I's daughter (Junagadh inscription).
- Yajna Sri Satakarni (c. 165–194 CE) was the last great ruler; recovered Malwa and Konkan.
- Both left ship-motif coins showing overseas trade.
- After Yajna Sri the empire fragmented.
keyPoints: Pulumavi pushed the southern frontier to the mouth of the Krishna River.
Pulumavi's ship-motif coins point to overseas trade.
Pulumavi married Rudradaman I's daughter (Junagadh inscription) — marital diplomacy.
Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great ruler; recovered Malwa and Konkan.
Yajna Sri's ship coins underline the era's maritime trade.
items.mnemonic: Pulumavi = 'ship coins + Rudradaman's daughter (Junagadh)'; Yajna Sri = 'last great, ships again'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Vashisthiputra Pulumavi; Yajna Sri Satakarni)

items.title: Matronymic Names & the Position of Women
items.body:
## Naming Kings After Their Mothers

**In one line:** Satavahana kings were often named after their mothers (a matronymic), which is taken as a sign that women held an unusually high place in that society.

**The story**
Most ancient dynasties named a prince after his father. The Satavahanas did the opposite: they used a **matronymic** — a name formed from the **mother's** name. So **Gautami-putra** means 'son of Gautami' and **Vashishti-putra** means 'son of Vashishti'. This was not just naming fashion. Real women wielded power: **Nayanika (Naganika)** acted as **regent**, ruling for her minor son, and **Gautami Balashri** composed the **Nasik Prashasti** that glorified her son Gautamiputra. Together these show women could govern and could shape the public record.

**Why it is asked**
'What does matronymic naming show?' and the Nayanika/Gautami Balashri examples are favourite culture-and-society questions.

**Picture it**

| Name | Means | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| Gautami-putra | Son of Gautami | Named after the mother |
| Vashishti-putra | Son of Vashishti | Named after the mother |
| Nayanika | Queen-regent | Woman ruling for a minor son |
| Gautami Balashri | Author of Nasik Prashasti | Woman shaping royal records |

**Terms explained**
- **Matronymic** — a name taken from the mother ('-putra' = 'son of'); the opposite is a patronymic (from the father).
- **Regent** — a person who rules on behalf of a king who is too young.

**Don't confuse**
- Matronymic naming means named after the **mother**, NOT the father, a deity or the capital city.
- Society still broadly followed the **varna** order; high status of women did not overturn caste.

**Remember it:** '-putra of the mother — Gautami-putra, Vashishti-putra: the mother gives the name'.

**TL;DR**
- Satavahana kings used matronymic names (Gautami-putra, Vashishti-putra).
- This points to the high status of women.
- Nayanika ruled as regent; Gautami Balashri authored the Nasik Prashasti.
- Society otherwise followed the varna system.
keyPoints: Matronymic tradition: kings named after their mothers (e.g. Gautami-putra, Vashishti-putra).
Reflects the high status of women in Satavahana society.
Nayanika (Naganika) acted as regent for her minor son.
Gautami Balashri authored the Nasik Prashasti.
items.mnemonic: 'Putra of the mother' — Gautami-putra, Vashishti-putra: matronymic names.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Social Structure – Matronymic Tradition; Position of Women)

items.title: Administration — Divisions, Feudatories & Officers
items.body:
## How the Satavahanas Governed

**In one line:** The Satavahanas kept the Mauryan habit of dividing land into provinces and districts, but added a layer of ranked feudatory chiefs, the top of whom could even mint their own coins.

**The story**
The Satavahanas borrowed the Mauryan idea of a tiered administration but loosened it to suit the wide, varied Deccan. The land was split, from largest to smallest, into **Janapada (province) → Rashtra (sub-province) → Ahara (district) → Vishaya (sub-division) → Grama (village)**. Below the king sat **feudatories** — semi-independent chiefs graded into three ranks: **Rajas** (the highest, who struck coins in their own names), **Mahabhojas** (strong in the Thane–Kolaba region) and **Maharathis** (around Poona). Villages were run by a **Gramani** or the military **Gaulmika**, and specialist officers handled money, water and works.

**Why it is asked**
The division order (Janapada to Grama) and the feudatory ranking (Rajas > Mahabhojas > Maharathis) are classic match-the-column and ordering questions.

**Picture it**

| Level | Unit / Rank | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Province | Janapada | Largest division |
| Sub-province | Rashtra | Under a Rashtrika/Maharathi |
| District | Ahara | Under Amatyas/Mahamatras |
| Sub-division | Vishaya | Smaller unit |
| Village | Grama | Under Gramani/Gaulmika |
| Feudatory 1 | Raja | Highest; minted own coins |
| Feudatory 2 | Mahabhoja | Thane–Kolaba |
| Feudatory 3 | Maharathi | Poona region |

**Terms explained**
- **Feudatory** — a local chief who accepts the king's overlordship but rules his own area.
- **Senapati** — commander of the army who also served as a provincial governor.
- **Rajjuka** — revenue officer; **Bhandagarika** — treasurer; **Paniyagharika** — officer of waterworks; **Karmantika** — public works; **Avesanika** — foreman of artisans.

**Don't confuse**
- Among feudatories, only the **Rajas** (highest grade) minted coins — not Mahabhojas or Maharathis.
- **Ahara** = district (an administrative unit); do not read it as a feudatory rank.

**Remember it:** Divisions big to small — 'Ja-Ra-A-Vi-Gra' (Janapada, Rashtra, Ahara, Vishaya, Grama); feudatories 'Raja > Mahabhoja > Maharathi'.

**TL;DR**
- Divisions (largest to smallest): Janapada > Rashtra > Ahara > Vishaya > Grama.
- Three feudatory grades: Rajas (minted coins) > Mahabhojas > Maharathis.
- Senapati was both army commander and provincial governor.
- Specialist officers: Rajjuka (revenue), Bhandagarika (treasury), Paniyagharika (water), Karmantika (works).
keyPoints: Divisions: Janapada > Rashtra > Ahara > Vishaya > Grama.
Three feudatory grades: Rajas (minted coins), Mahabhojas, Maharathis.
Gaulmika/Gramani headed villages; Katakas & Skandhavaras were military camps/cantonments.
Senapati served as both army commander and provincial governor.
Specialist officers: Rajjuka (revenue), Bhandagarika (treasury), Paniyagharika (water), Karmantika (works).
items.mnemonic: Divisions big→small: 'Ja-Ra-A-Vi-Gra' (Janapada, Rashtra, Ahara, Vishaya, Grama).

items.title: Economy, Trade & Coinage
items.body:
## A Trading Powerhouse

**In one line:** The Satavahana economy rested on the rich Krishna–Godavari rice lands and on brisk land-and-sea trade, which is why their coins — mostly lead — carry ship and animal motifs.

**The story**
Two things made the Satavahanas wealthy. First, **agriculture**: the **Krishna–Godavari delta** was a great **rice bowl**, and **paddy transplantation** (moving seedlings into flooded fields) raised yields. Second, **trade**: goods moved along the **Uttarapatha** (the northern route) and the **Dakshinapatha** (the southern route), and out through western **ports** such as **Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch (Barygaza) and Ganjam**. The dynasty minted coins mainly in **lead** (also **copper, bronze and potin**) with **Prakrit legends in the Brahmi script** and designs of **animals, ships and Chaityas**. The ship design is a direct clue to flourishing **maritime trade**, including trade with the **Roman world** through Barygaza.

**Why it is asked**
'What metal were Satavahana coins?' (lead), the ship motif, and the port names are standard economy facts and discrimination questions.

**Picture it**

| Pillar | Detail |
|---|---|
| Agriculture | Krishna–Godavari rice bowl; paddy transplantation |
| Trade routes | Uttarapatha (north), Dakshinapatha (south) |
| Ports | Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch (Barygaza), Ganjam |
| Coin metals | Lead (mainly), copper, bronze, potin |
| Coin designs | Animals, ships, Chaityas; Prakrit in Brahmi |
| Foreign link | Roman trade via Barygaza |

**Terms explained**
- **Uttarapatha / Dakshinapatha** — the main northern and southern trade highways of ancient India.
- **Barygaza** — the Greek-Roman name for the port of Bharuch in Gujarat.
- **Potin** — a base-metal alloy (copper, tin, lead) used for some coins.
- **Chaitya** — a Buddhist prayer hall / stupa shape, shown on some coins.

**Don't confuse**
- Satavahana coins were mainly **lead**, NOT gold or silver; large-scale gold coinage came later (Kushanas/Guptas).
- **Tamralipti** (in Bengal) was a famous port but NOT a Satavahana port — their ports were western (Sopara, Kalyani, Bharuch, Ganjam).

**Remember it:** 'Satavahana money = lead coins with ships' — the sea-trade dynasty of the rice delta.

**TL;DR**
- Krishna–Godavari delta was a major rice bowl; paddy transplantation raised yields.
- Trade on the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha; ports Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch, Ganjam.
- Coins mainly in lead (also copper, bronze, potin), with Prakrit (Brahmi) legends.
- Ship-and-Chaitya designs show maritime trade, including with Rome.
keyPoints: Krishna–Godavari delta was a major rice bowl; paddy transplantation raised yields.
Trade along Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha; ports: Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch, Ganjam.
Coins in lead, copper and bronze with animal motifs and Prakrit (Brahmi) legends.
Ship-and-Chaitya coins reflect thriving maritime trade (incl. Roman contact via Barygaza).
items.mnemonic: Satavahana money = 'Lead & copper coins with ships' — the sea-trade dynasty.

items.title: Art & Architecture — The Amaravati School
items.body:
## Deccan Buddhist Art (AP relevance)

**In one line:** Satavahana patronage produced the Amaravati Stupa in Andhra Pradesh — the heart of a whole sculptural style, the Amaravati School — plus rock-cut Buddhist monuments in Maharashtra.

**The story**
The Satavahanas were Hindu kings who nonetheless poured wealth into **Buddhist art**. Their showpiece is the **Amaravati Stupa** on the Krishna in Andhra Pradesh, begun in the **3rd century BCE** and faced with white marble reliefs showing **Jataka tales (stories of the Buddha's past lives) and scenes from the Buddha's life**. It was brought to modern attention by **Colin Mackenzie**, the first Surveyor General of India, and it gives its name to the famous **Amaravati School of Art**. Close by, **Nagarjunakonda** — later enriched under the **Ikshvakus** — carries fine Buddhist carvings. In the western Deccan, the **Karle Chaitya** is the **largest rock-cut Chaitya hall**, and **Ajanta Caves 9 and 10** were cut under Satavahana patronage.

**Why it is asked**
Amaravati = AP's flagship ancient monument; its discovery by Colin Mackenzie and the match of monument-to-location are heavily tested.

**Picture it**

| Monument | Location | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Amaravati Stupa | Andhra Pradesh | Discovered by Colin Mackenzie; Amaravati School |
| Nagarjunakonda | Andhra Pradesh | Later Ikshvaku patronage |
| Karle Chaitya | Maharashtra | Largest rock-cut Chaitya hall |
| Ajanta Caves 9 & 10 | Maharashtra | Early, under Satavahana patronage |

**Terms explained**
- **Stupa** — a dome-shaped Buddhist monument holding relics.
- **Chaitya** — a Buddhist prayer hall, often rock-cut, with a stupa at the far end.
- **Jataka tales** — stories of the Buddha's previous births, carved as narrative panels.
- **Colin Mackenzie** — the first Surveyor General of India, who recorded Amaravati.

**Don't confuse**
- The early **Ajanta Caves 9 and 10** are Satavahana; the famous later caves (1, 2, 16, 17, 26) belong to the **Vakataka (Gupta-age)** phase.
- **Amaravati** (Satavahana) and **Nagarjunakonda** (mainly Ikshvaku) are different sites, both in AP.

**Remember it:** 'AP's Buddhist gems — Amaravati + Nagarjunakonda; Maharashtra's rock-cut — Karle + Ajanta 9-10'.

**TL;DR**
- Amaravati Stupa (AP): Jataka tales and the Buddha's life; discovered by Colin Mackenzie; namesake of the Amaravati School.
- Nagarjunakonda (AP): Buddhist carvings, later under the Ikshvakus.
- Karle Chaitya (Maharashtra): largest rock-cut Chaitya hall.
- Ajanta Caves 9 and 10: early, under Satavahana patronage.

figure.caption: Amaravati (Krishna valley, Andhra Pradesh) gave its name to the Amaravati School of Art — a hallmark of Satavahana-era Buddhist sculpture.

keyPoints: Amaravati Stupa (AP): Jataka tales & Buddha's life; discovered by Colin Mackenzie — namesake of the Amaravati School of Art.
Nagarjunakonda (AP): Buddhist carvings, later patronised by the Ikshvakus.
Karle Chaitya (Maharashtra): largest rock-cut Chaitya hall.
Ajanta Caves 9 and 10 developed under Satavahana patronage.

items.title: Religion, Society & Land Grants to Brahmins
items.body:
## Brahmanism with Buddhist Patronage

**In one line:** The Satavahana kings were Brahmins who performed Vedic sacrifices, yet they also funded Buddhism through land grants — and in doing so they pioneered the practice of gifting land that shaped later Indian history.

**The story**
The Satavahanas show how a dynasty could back two faiths at once. As **Brahmins**, the kings performed grand **Vedic sacrifices** such as the **Ashvamedha and Rajasuya** to display their status. At the same time, they **gave land grants to Buddhist monks** and monasteries. These grants — often with tax-free and administrative privileges — were an **early model of the land-grant system** that spread across India in later centuries. Socially, the **varna system** ordered society, but because trade was booming, **merchants and artisans** rose in importance and formed guilds. Women, as the matronymic names show, held a relatively high place.

**Why it is asked**
The 'Brahmin kings who funded Buddhism' paradox, and land grants as a historical first, are standard society-and-religion points.

**Picture it**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Royal faith | Brahmanism; Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Rajasuya) |
| Also funded | Buddhism — land grants to monks |
| Historical first | Early land-grant tradition with privileges |
| Society | Varna order; rising merchants and artisans |
| Women | Relatively high status (matronymics, regents) |

**Terms explained**
- **Rajasuya** — a Vedic royal consecration sacrifice.
- **Land grant** — a gift of land (often tax-free) to a priest, monk or monastery.
- **Varna** — the four-fold ordering of society (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra).

**Don't confuse**
- The kings were **Brahmins by faith** but still **patrons of Buddhism** — supporting Buddhism did not make them Buddhist.
- Land grants went to **both** Brahmins and Buddhist monks, not to one group only.

**Remember it:** 'Brahmin kings, Buddhist land grants' — faith balance and the first land-grant tradition.

**TL;DR**
- Rulers were Brahmins performing Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Rajasuya).
- They also patronised Buddhism through land grants to monks.
- Pioneered the land-grant tradition with fiscal privileges.
- Varna society, but traders and artisans gained importance through trade.
keyPoints: Rulers were Brahmins performing Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Rajasuya).
Simultaneously patronised Buddhism through land grants to monks.
Early practice of land grants (to Brahmins/monasteries) with privileges.
Varna society, but traders and artisans rose in importance due to trade.
items.mnemonic: Satavahana faith balance — 'Brahmin kings, Buddhist land grants'.

items.title: Decline & Successor Kingdoms
items.body:
## The End of Satavahana Rule

**In one line:** After the last strong king, weak rulers and ambitious feudatories broke the empire into regional successor states — the Ikshvakus taking over the Andhra heartland.

**The story**
Every empire has a tipping point. For the Satavahanas it came after **Yajna Sri Satakarni**: the kings who followed were **weak**, and the very **feudatories** the dynasty had relied on now **broke away** and seized power for themselves. As central authority dissolved, the land split into **successor kingdoms**. In **Andhra Pradesh** the **Ikshvakus** took charge (continuing Buddhist patronage at Nagarjunakonda). In the **Maharashtra / western Deccan** the **Abhiras and Chutus** rose, and in **Tamil Nadu** the **Pallavas** came up.

**Why it is asked**
'Who succeeded the Satavahanas in Andhra?' (the Ikshvakus) is a direct link-question that also bridges into the next AP topic.

**Picture it**

| Successor | Region |
|---|---|
| Ikshvakus | Andhra Pradesh (Krishna–Guntur) |
| Abhiras | Maharashtra / western Deccan |
| Chutus | Maharashtra / western Deccan |
| Pallavas | Tamil Nadu |

**Terms explained**
- **Feudatory** — a subordinate chief; here they grew strong enough to break the empire.
- **Ikshvakus** — the dynasty that ruled the Andhra region immediately after the Satavahanas.

**Don't confuse**
- In **Andhra Pradesh** the successors were the **Ikshvakus**, NOT the Pallavas (who rose in Tamil Nadu).
- The **Abhiras and Chutus** rose in **Maharashtra**, not in the Andhra heartland.

**Remember it:** 'After the Satavahanas — Ikshvakus (AP), Abhiras/Chutus (Maharashtra), Pallavas (TN)'.

**TL;DR**
- Decline set in with weak rulers after Yajna Sri Satakarni.
- Rising feudatories and lost central authority fragmented the empire.
- Ikshvakus succeeded in Andhra Pradesh.
- Abhiras and Chutus rose in Maharashtra; Pallavas in Tamil Nadu.
keyPoints: Decline set in with weak rulers after Yajna Sri Satakarni.
Rising feudatories and lost central authority fragmented the empire.
Ikshvakus succeeded in Andhra Pradesh.
Abhiras and Chutus rose in Maharashtra; Pallavas in Tamil Nadu.

items.title: For Mains — Satavahanas (Post-Mauryan Deccan)
items.body:
## For Mains — the Satavahanas as a theme

Mains (Paper-II, General Studies, clause M2-1b: Satavahanas, Sangam, Sungas, Guptas) rarely wants a king-list. It wants you to argue **why the Satavahanas matter** — as the force that reunified the Deccan, Indianised the south, and seeded institutions (land grants, maritime trade, Prakrit culture) that outlived them. Frame answers around dimensions, not chronology.

**Dimensions the question can take**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Political role | First post-Mauryan Deccan empire; bridge between a fragmenting north and the far south; absorbed Shaka pressure (Gautamiputra vs Nahapana) |
| Economy | Krishna–Godavari rice surplus; Indo-Roman trade via Barygaza/Sopara; lead coinage and guild-based crafts |
| Religion & society | Brahmin kings performing Ashvamedha yet endowing Buddhist sanghas — model of accommodation; pioneering land grants (agraharas) |
| Culture | Prakrit as court language (Hala's Gatha Saptasati); Amaravati school of sculpture |
| Women | Matronymics, Nayanika's regency, Gautami Balashri's prashasti — comparatively high status |
| Legacy / limits | Land grants began the slide toward feudal fragmentation that ended the dynasty |

**Data points / sources to quote**
- **Nasik Prashasti** of Gautami Balashri — empire from Malwa/Saurashtra/Konkan to the Krishna; title Ekabrahmana.
- **Naneghat inscription** (Queen Nayanika) — Satakarni I, Vedic sacrifices, women's status.
- **Junagadh inscription** of Rudradaman I — Satavahana–Shaka marital diplomacy.
- **Periplus of the Erythraean Sea** / Ptolemy — Roman trade through Barygaza and the Deccan ports.
- **Amaravati & Nagarjunakonda** — Buddhist art and the land-grant tradition.

**AP angle**
The Puranas call them the **Andhras**; Amaravati was a capital and gave AP its signature art school; the Ikshvaku successors deepened Buddhism at Nagarjunakonda — so for APPSC the Satavahanas are the opening chapter of Andhra's imperial story.

**Use in answers**
- Open with the 'bridge' thesis: 'The Satavahanas reunified the post-Mauryan Deccan and Indianised the peninsula.'
- Quote the Nasik Prashasti for both conquest AND tolerance in one line.
- Diagram idea: a two-axis sketch — trade routes (Uttarapatha/Dakshinapatha + sea) crossing the religion axis (Brahmanism + Buddhism) to show synthesis.
- Close with the irony that land grants, their great innovation, also hastened their decline.
keyPoints: Thesis: Satavahanas reunified the post-Mauryan Deccan and bridged north and south.
Quote the Nasik Prashasti for conquest (vs Nahapana) and religious tolerance together.
Economy: Indo-Roman trade via Barygaza/Sopara; lead coinage; rice surplus.
Religion: Brahmin kings endowing Buddhist sanghas; pioneering land grants (agraharas).
AP angle: 'Andhras' of the Puranas; Amaravati capital and art school; Ikshvaku successors.
Critique: land grants seeded the feudal fragmentation that ended the dynasty.
